title: Same development cost, but scale crushes: Costco can't catch up to Sam's Club in China
dek: Sam's invested in supply chain and product development early, turning it into a scale advantage; Costco pays equal development costs but suppliers get only a fraction of Sam's order volumes—money can't bridge that gap.
why: Breaks down the specific mechanics and numbers behind why Sam's wins and why Costco can't catch up in China; plus dissects the distinct playbooks of Jinglilimen (金粒门), Aldi, and Woji Select, with high information density.
who: Retail operators, consumer brand builders, supply chain businesses, and consumer investors who want to understand the economics behind warehouse and discount formats like Sam's Club, Aldi, and Jinglilimen.
skip: First three minutes of guest introduction and Moxiaoxian (莫小仙) brand background—not essential for understanding China's supermarket competitive landscape.

points.h: First-mover wins scale: same development cost, ten times the order volume
points.body: Sam's and Costco pay identical product development costs—testing, labor, recipe sampling—but Sam's suppliers might receive 60–100 million yuan orders per SKU while Costco suppliers get only 5–10 million yuan. Fixed costs amortize differently across volume; Sam's spreads them over larger orders while Costco can't. Sam's also cherry-picked the best suppliers first; Costco works with whoever's left. That gap can't be closed with spending.

points.h: Supermarkets once thrived on rental fees, not sales margins
points.body: Traditional Chinese supermarkets inherited a Taiwan retail model: checkout codes, entry fees, promotion fees, poster fees—sometimes 500–1,000 yuan per SKU per store, plus holiday surcharges. Traditional hypermarkets' gross margins hit 20–30%, nearly double Sam's, but most came from supplier fees, not actual retail spread. Warehouse clubs like Sam's collect almost none of these fees and make profit entirely on sales margins, forcing them to genuinely care who the customer is and what they need—not who pays to get shelved.

points.h: Retail has no secrets; excellence gets copied immediately
points.body: As Buffett and Munger note, retail is hard and has few secrets—when you do it well, competitors copy. Today's new Chinese supermarkets increasingly look alike: richer assortments, better visuals, smoother flow. Jinglilimen's fresh presentation, Sam's warehouse style—everyone borrows them. As SKU inventories converge and supplier rosters become transparent, 200–300 SKUs are easily replicated. Competition ultimately hinges on operational efficiency and cost discipline, not innovation.

points.h: Jinglilimen undersells Sam's Club on the exact same mochi snack
points.body: Jinglilimen and Jiduo Qi (几多鸡), both based in Changsha, drained foot traffic from Sam's at Hangzhou's Xixi Impression City this year. Price checks show Jinglilimen's mochi at 1.1 yuan per piece—cheaper than Sam's. Shelf visuals and T-shaped transparent box design are also superior. The gap suggests Sam's supply chain isn't optimized: the company relies on a fixed roster of suppliers that rarely admit newcomers, leaving room for flexible competitors to hit lower prices and better aesthetics. These short-shelf-life models without membership fees are called ‘Sam's without the card.’

points.h: China's Aldi is not America's low-income discount store
points.body: Aldi operates in rural-urban fringe zones in the US and Germany; in New York, you see wilted cabbage, serving lower-income shoppers. China's Aldi is entirely different: it sits inside malls facing white-collar workers and young professionals. Bowl combos, salads, cold desserts—better executed than traditional hypermarkets. It's best framed as a middle-class budget store, closer to Trader Joe's than American Aldi. Over 90% private label, transitioning from raw ingredients to authentic taste—partnering with heritage brands to restore traditional flavors.

points.h: Developing a private label product costs 150,000 yuan and four months
points.body: Creating a new PB product for retailers like Hema (盒马) takes three to four months from concept to launch. Direct project labor alone runs 150,000 yuan, not counting testing, prototyping, packaging, and later promotion. This barrier means factories without R&D teams and supply chain depth can't take the order. Retailers now demand you define products, not just pay for shelf space. Industry convention suggests a 70:30 or 80:20 ratio of classics to novelties; but novelties cost equally to develop and scale slower, creating hard ROI tradeoffs.

points.h: Walmart's private labels look polished but give no reason to repeat
points.body: Chengdu's new Woji Select (沃集选) shows sophisticated curation, naming, value propositions, and visual design—excellent seeding on Little Red Book and Douyin. But it's missing one thing: a reason to come back. Name one Walmart private label that's exclusive to Walmart, one you must buy there. His actual shopping: olive oil and beef at Sam's Club, or vegetables and Hunan smoked salt-cured pork at Ding Ding (丁盯) because the latter's range is complete and flavors are unbeatable and irreplaceable. Walmart's classic PLs match competitors closely—first purchase driven by trend content, but repurchase doesn't stick.

points.h: Japanese supermarkets stratify by income; same curry, three price tiers
points.body: In Osaka, the same 180–200 gram curry beef package sells at 100 yen in discount chains, 300 yen midmarket, and 680 yen in premium stores—all healthy sellers, because they serve different income groups' competing versions of the same need. Premium is short-shelf cold storage, midmarket gets brand partnerships and upgrades, budget solves the basic problem. China's retail endgame will mirror this layered ecosystem: hard discounters, soft discounters, budget stores, mid-market, and luxury all coexisting, not one format claiming everyone.

Pre-designed display case: factory-packed cartons designed to go straight to shelf without repacking, saving labor.

quotes.text: If you try to replicate Sam's, you can't catch them, because Sam's has first-mover advantages—their supply chain edge, their low per-unit development costs—which you lack. If Costco copies Sam's approach to chase Sam's in China, it's impossible to catch up.
It changed over time. Actually, it did start to shift—at first there was a rental-fee model, but later it moved to a sales-driven logic. Everyone's been through this transition, so China is too.

Their mochi—nine pieces for 9.9 yuan—that's really well done. It's basically taking Sam's bulk box and breaking it into smaller pieces at the same price per piece. But their mochi sells for 1.1 yuan each. How much is Sam's? Sam's can't compete with them on price. Sam's isn't even cheaper—it costs more, much more.
Got it—it's a budget supermarket for the middle class, not the American discount chain.

Developing a product for Hema—here's what it requires: a one-time investment. In labor costs alone, if you count four months of work, about 150,000 yuan. That's the one-time cost. We're not even talking about whether it sells or not.

Products are how you talk to the consumer—and I'm here to buy things. So Walmart made a ton of private labels. Tell me: of all the products Walmart has created, which do you think are exclusive to Walmart, that you must buy from them? What product gives you a reason to shop at Walmart? Name one.

Take curry beef—about 180–200 grams. In a premium store it sells for 680 yen, roughly 30 yuan. But go to a discount supermarket, it's only 100 yen. Go to mid-market, it's 300 yen. Same curry beef sauce, same size, from 100 yen to 300 yen to 680 yen—all sell well.
